pinecone: Which Pinecone index type needs no choice of pod type or pod count and scales automatically with usage?
A serverless index
A pod-based index on p1 pods
A pod-based index on s1 pods
A pod-based index on p2 pods
Serverless indexes manage capacity for you. Pod-based indexes require you to choose pod type, size, pods and replicas.
In Pinecone, what is a namespace?
A partition inside one index that upserts and queries target
A separate project with its own API key, users and billing plan
A metadata field that every record must include
A replica group that serves queries in one region
Namespaces split the records of one index into isolated partitions. A query searches a single namespace.
Which three similarity metrics can you choose when creating a Pinecone dense index?
cosine, euclidean, dotproduct
cosine, manhattan, hamming
jaccard, euclidean, dotproduct
cosine, chebyshev, euclidean
Pinecone dense indexes support cosine, euclidean and dotproduct, chosen when the index is created.
In Pinecone, what happens when you upsert a record whose id already exists in the same namespace?
The existing record is replaced by the new one
The request fails with a duplicate id error
A second record with the same id is stored
Only the metadata changes and the vector is ignored
Upsert means insert or overwrite: a matching id in the namespace is replaced with the new vector and metadata.
What does the top_k parameter control in a Pinecone query?
How many of the most similar records are returned
How many namespaces are searched in parallel per query
The minimum score a match must reach
How many replicas answer each query
top_k sets the number of nearest matches returned. It is not a score threshold.
A Pinecone index was created with dimension 1536. What happens if you upsert 768-dimensional vectors into it?
The upsert is rejected because the dimension does not match
Pinecone pads the vectors with zeros up to 1536 dimensions
Pinecone shrinks the index dimension to 768 to match
The vectors are stored but silently skipped by all later queries
Every vector must match the dimension fixed at index creation, so mismatched vectors are rejected.
Which Pinecone metadata filter matches records whose genre is either comedy or drama?
{"genre": {"$in": ["comedy", "drama"]}}
{"genre": {"$or": ["comedy", "drama"]}}
{"$and": [{"genre": "comedy"}, {"genre": "drama"}]}
{"genre": {"$nin": ["comedy", "drama"]}}
$in matches any listed value. $or combines whole conditions rather than values, $and would require both at once, and $nin excludes them.
Which Pinecone metadata filter keeps only records with year 2020 or later?
$gte means greater than or equal and is placed under the field name. $gt would exclude 2020 itself.
A SaaS app stores every customer's vectors in one Pinecone serverless index and must isolate customers and delete one customer's data easily. What fits best?
One namespace per customer
One similarity metric per customer
All customers in the default namespace
One index dimension per customer
Namespaces isolate tenants within an index, queries only see one namespace, and a whole namespace can be deleted at once.
What does include_metadata=True add to a Pinecone query response?
Each match's stored metadata next to its id and score
A filter that keeps only records that have metadata
The index configuration, such as metric and dimension
Metadata from every namespace in the index
By default matches carry ids and scores. include_metadata (and include_values) add the stored metadata (and vectors).
You need to load 5 million vectors into Pinecone through the upsert API. Which approach is recommended?
Batch records per request and send batches in parallel
Send exactly one record per request, sequentially
Put all 5 million records into one single request
Recreate the index after every uploaded batch
Batching reduces per-request overhead and parallel requests raise throughput. Requests have a size limit, so one giant request fails.
Right after a Pinecone upsert returns success, a query does not show the new record yet. What is the usual reason?
Writes are eventually consistent and may need a moment
Writes stay invisible until an explicit commit call
Queries read only from a nightly index snapshot
New records appear only after an index restart
Pinecone is eventually consistent: freshly upserted records can take a short time before they are queryable.
Which Pinecone index operation returns the record count for each namespace?
describe_index_stats
describe_index
describe_collection
list_indexes
describe_index_stats reports total and per-namespace record counts. describe_index returns configuration such as dimension, metric and host, and describe_collection describes a static collection.
A pod-based Pinecone index has enough storage but cannot handle the query load. What raises queries per second?
Adding replicas to the index
Changing the metric to dotproduct
Spreading records over more namespaces
Lowering the index dimension
In pod-based indexes, replicas serve copies of the data and add query throughput, while pods and pod size add capacity.
In Pinecone pod-based indexes, how do s1 pods differ from p1 pods?
s1 holds more vectors per pod, p1 has lower latency
s1 runs on GPUs for speed, p1 runs on CPUs only
s1 stores only sparse vectors, p1 only dense vectors
s1 is serverless, p1 is a dedicated provisioned pod
s1 pods are storage optimized with higher latency. p1 pods are performance optimized with less capacity per pod.
You want sparse-dense (hybrid) vectors in a single Pinecone index. Which metric must the index use?
dotproduct
cosine
euclidean
manhattan
Pinecone supports querying sparse-dense vectors only on indexes that use the dotproduct metric.
Your embedding model outputs unit-length vectors. Which statement about Pinecone metric choice is true?
cosine and dotproduct rank the results identically
euclidean gives the reverse ranking of cosine
dotproduct needs vectors of differing lengths
cosine works only on sparse vectors
For unit vectors the dot product equals cosine similarity, so both give the same ordering (euclidean also agrees).
Which metadata value can a Pinecone record NOT store for filtering?
{"author": {"name": "Ann"}}
{"genre": "crime drama"}
{"published": 2021}
{"tags": ["ai", "vector-db"]}
Pinecone metadata supports strings, numbers, booleans and lists of strings. Nested objects are not supported.
Which statement about Pinecone serverless indexes is accurate?
Storage and compute are separated and billing follows usage
You must choose a pod size from x1 to x8 before creating it
All vectors live only in RAM on dedicated pods
It cannot be split into separate namespaces
Serverless indexes decouple storage from compute and charge for reads, writes and storage instead of provisioned pods.
Which setting of an existing Pinecone index cannot be changed after creation?
The similarity metric
Deletion protection
The replica count (pod-based)
The tags on the index
Metric and dimension are fixed at creation. Deletion protection, tags and pod-based replicas can be changed with configure_index.
weaviate: In Weaviate, what is a class (called a collection in the v4 client)?
A named set of objects sharing properties and vector config
A single JSON object stored together with its own vector and id
A user role that groups permissions on the whole server
A backup archive of the whole database and its schema
A class or collection defines the properties, vectorizer and vector index settings shared by its objects.
A Weaviate class is configured with vectorizer set to none. What does that mean?
You supply the vectors yourself when importing objects
Weaviate falls back to text2vec-transformers for every import
Only BM25 keyword queries work on the class
Weaviate picks a vectorizer for each query
With no vectorizer, Weaviate does not create embeddings, so you bring your own. nearVector still works on those vectors.
What does a Weaviate hybrid search combine?
BM25 keyword search and vector search
Two vectorizers applied to one property
Results from the GraphQL and REST APIs
Results from an HNSW and a flat index
Hybrid search fuses the ranked results of a BM25 keyword search and a vector similarity search.
In a Weaviate hybrid query, what does alpha: 0 mean?
Pure keyword (BM25) search
Pure vector (HNSW) search
Equal keyword and vector weight
The query is rejected as invalid
alpha weights vector against keyword results: 1 is pure vector search and 0 is pure keyword search.
In a Weaviate hybrid query, what does alpha: 0.5 mean?
Keyword and vector results are weighted equally
Only half of the objects are searched
Results scoring under 0.5 are dropped
The vector search uses only half of the vector dimensions
alpha is the vector weight and 1 minus alpha is the keyword weight, so 0.5 balances both.
What is the default distance metric of a Weaviate vector index?
cosine
dot
l2-squared
manhattan
Weaviate uses cosine distance unless you set another metric in the vector index config.
Which Weaviate search operator requires a vectorizer module configured on the class?
nearText
nearVector
nearObject
bm25
nearText turns query text into a vector, which needs a vectorizer. nearVector takes your vector and nearObject reuses a stored one.
Which Weaviate GraphQL query returns the total number of Article objects?
{ Aggregate { Article { meta { count } } } }
{ Get { Article { meta { count } } } }
{ Count { Article { total } } }
{ Get { Article { _additional { count } } } }
Aggregate computes statistics such as meta { count }. Get returns objects, not aggregated counts.
In a Weaviate GraphQL Get query with nearText, where do you request each result's distance?
In the _additional { distance } field
As a top-level argument distance: true
Inside the where filter of the query
In a meta { distance } sub-field
Search metadata such as distance, certainty, id and vector is returned through the _additional field.
Which Weaviate where-filter operator selects objects whose wordCount is more than 1000?
GreaterThan with valueInt: 1000
Above with valueInt: 1000
MoreThan with valueInt: 1000
Gt with valueInt: 1000
Weaviate filter operators include Equal, NotEqual, GreaterThan, GreaterThanEqual, LessThan, LessThanEqual and Like.
How do you require two conditions to both match in a Weaviate where filter?
Use operator And with both conditions in operands
Put both property names into one path array
Pass two separate where arguments to Get
Use operator Both with a valueText list
Conditions are combined with the And or Or operator, listing the individual conditions in operands.
How does Weaviate apply a where filter together with a vector search?
It builds an allow-list from the inverted index, then searches within it
It runs the vector search first, then drops results that fail the filter
It ignores the filter whenever a query vector is given
It runs one query per filter value and merges the results
Weaviate pre-filters: matching ids come from the inverted index first, so filtering does not shrink the result count like post-filtering.
In Weaviate multi-tenancy, what does each tenant get?
Its own shard, isolating its data from other tenants
Its own schema, with properties that differ from other tenants
Its own dedicated vectorizer module instance
Its own separate GraphQL endpoint and API key
Tenants share the class schema, but each tenant's data lives in a separate shard that can be managed and deleted independently.
A Weaviate class has multi-tenancy enabled. What happens if you insert an object without naming a tenant?
The request fails because a tenant is required
The object goes to a default tenant
The object is copied to every tenant
The object lands in a shared global shard instead
On a multi-tenant class every read and write must specify the tenant.
In Weaviate, a tenant's activity status is set to INACTIVE (COLD in older versions). What happens?
Its data stays on disk but cannot be queried until reactivated
Its objects are deleted permanently after one day of inactivity
It stays queryable but rejects all new writes
Its objects are merged into the other tenants
Inactive tenants are not loaded into memory, saving resources, and become usable again once set back to ACTIVE.
With Weaviate's cosine metric, what does a result distance of 0 mean?
The vectors point in the same direction
The vectors point in opposite directions
The vectors are orthogonal to each other
The object has no vector stored
Cosine distance is 1 minus cosine similarity, so 0 means identical direction and 2 means opposite.
In Weaviate, the certainty value is only available with which distance metric?
cosine
dot
l2-squared
hamming
certainty is a normalized score derived from cosine distance. For other metrics, use distance instead.
With auto-schema enabled, what happens when you import an object with a property the Weaviate class does not define?
The property is added, with its type inferred from the value
The import fails with an unknown property error for that object
The property is silently dropped from the object
The value is stored as an untyped binary blob
Auto-schema extends the class on import and infers data types. Disabling it makes unknown properties an error.
Which Weaviate data type fits a property storing a price such as 19.99?
number
int
float
text
Weaviate uses number for floating point values and int for integers. There is no data type called float.
Which kind of Weaviate module lets you run retrieval augmented generation on search results?
A generative module such as generative-openai
A vectorizer module such as text2vec-cohere
A backup module such as backup-s3
An image module such as img2vec-neural
Generative modules send retrieved objects to an LLM with a prompt. Vectorizer modules only create embeddings.
qdrant: What is a point in Qdrant?
A record with an id, vectors and an optional payload
A single shard replica placed on one node of the cluster
A named layer inside the HNSW graph of a collection
A payload index built on one field of a collection's points
Collections hold points. Each point has an id, its vector or named vectors, and a JSON payload.
Which values can a Qdrant point id be?
An unsigned integer or a UUID
Any string up to 64 bytes long
Only integers assigned by Qdrant
A float or a timestamp
Qdrant accepts 64-bit unsigned integers and UUIDs as point ids. Arbitrary strings are rejected.
By default, on which port does Qdrant serve its gRPC API?
Qdrant listens on 6333 for REST (HTTP) and 6334 for gRPC by default.
Which QdrantClient argument makes the Python client use gRPC instead of REST where possible?
prefer_grpc=True
use_grpc=True
protocol="grpc"
grpc_only=True
QdrantClient(host=..., prefer_grpc=True) switches supported calls to gRPC, usually on port 6334.
Why might you choose Qdrant's gRPC API over REST for a large ingestion job?
Binary Protobuf messages are usually faster for bulk uploads
It is the only Qdrant API that supports filters
It is the only Qdrant API that creates snapshots
It skips authentication, which saves a round trip per request
REST and gRPC expose the same functionality, but gRPC's binary encoding has less overhead for large payloads.
When creating a Qdrant collection, which two vector parameters must you provide?
Vector size and distance metric
Shard count and replication factor
Payload schema and id format
HNSW m and ef_construct
VectorParams(size=..., distance=...) is required. Shards, replicas and HNSW settings have defaults.
Which of these is NOT a built-in distance metric in Qdrant?
Jaccard
Cosine
Dot
Euclid
Qdrant supports Cosine, Dot, Euclid and Manhattan distance.
How does Qdrant implement the Cosine distance for a collection?
It normalizes vectors on upload and then uses the dot product
It computes the arccos of each vector pair during every search
It converts Cosine into Euclid at query time
It applies Cosine only to quantized vectors
For unit vectors the dot product equals cosine similarity, so Qdrant normalizes once on insert to make search cheaper.
In a Qdrant filter, which clause means at least one of its conditions must match?
should
must
must_not
match_any
must requires all conditions, must_not excludes them, and should requires at least one.
Which Qdrant condition matches points whose city payload is London or Berlin?
{"key": "city", "match": {"any": ["London", "Berlin"]}}
{"key": "city", "match": {"value": ["London", "Berlin"]}}
{"key": "city", "match": {"except": ["London", "Berlin"]}}
{"key": "city", "range": {"any": ["London", "Berlin"]}}
match any is an IN condition. match value takes a single value, and except does the opposite.
Which Qdrant condition keeps points with price from 10 to 20, both ends included?
{"key": "price", "range": {"gte": 10, "lte": 20}}
{"key": "price", "range": {"gt": 10, "lt": 20}}
{"key": "price", "range": {"from": 10, "to": 20}}
{"key": "price", "match": {"value": [10, 20]}}
gte and lte include the bounds. gt and lt would exclude 10 and 20.
Qdrant searches filtered by user_id are slow on a large collection. What is the first fix to try?
Create a payload index on user_id
Increase the vector size of the collection
Switch the distance metric to Dot
Set HNSW m to 0 on the collection
A payload index (for example keyword type) speeds up filtering and lets the query planner choose an efficient strategy.
What is the effect of raising the HNSW m parameter in a Qdrant collection?
Higher recall, but more memory and slower index builds
Lower memory use, but noticeably lower recall on searches
Fewer vectors can be stored in the collection
Quantization is switched off for the collection
m is the number of edges per node. More edges make the graph denser and more accurate but heavier to build and store.
Which Qdrant search-time parameter raises HNSW accuracy at the cost of latency?
hnsw_ef
ef_construct
payload_m
full_scan_threshold
hnsw_ef sets the candidate list size during search. ef_construct and payload_m apply when the index is built, and full_scan_threshold decides when to skip the index.
Qdrant docs suggest setting HNSW m to 0 during a large initial upload. What does that do?
It skips building the HNSW graph until you restore m
It hides the uploaded points until you restore m
It deletes the existing graph and all payloads
It switches the collection to product quantization
With m = 0 no graph is built, so ingestion is faster. Setting m back afterwards builds the index once.
Roughly how much does Qdrant scalar quantization to int8 reduce vector memory compared to float32?
About 4 times
About 2 times
About 16 times
About 64 times
Each 4-byte float becomes a 1-byte integer, so memory drops by about 4x with a small accuracy loss.
With quantization enabled in Qdrant, what do the rescore and oversampling search options do?
Fetch extra candidates with quantized vectors, then rerank with originals
Retrain the quantizer on each query to adapt codebooks to the query
Copy every point to more shards so the query can run in parallel
Re-quantize stored vectors to fewer bits after every query
Oversampling retrieves more candidates using fast quantized vectors and rescoring reorders them with full-precision vectors to restore accuracy.
How does product quantization compare with scalar quantization in Qdrant?
It compresses more, but usually loses more accuracy
It is lossless, so search accuracy stays exactly the same
It compresses less but searches much faster
It works only on collections with GPU support
Product quantization can reach far higher compression ratios than int8 scalar quantization, at a larger cost in recall.
Which Qdrant REST call creates a snapshot of only the collection named docs?
POST /collections/docs/snapshots
POST /snapshots?collection=docs
GET /collections/docs/backup
PUT /collections/docs/snapshots/recover
POST /snapshots makes a full storage snapshot of all collections, and the recover endpoint restores from a snapshot instead of creating one.
In a distributed Qdrant cluster, what does a collection snapshot created on one node contain?
Only the shards of that collection stored on that node
Every shard of the collection, gathered from all the nodes
Only the collection config, without any points
The data of every collection in the cluster
Snapshots are per node in distributed mode, so a full backup means creating a snapshot on each node.
milvus: What is the role of the proxy in Milvus 2.x?
A stateless entry point that validates and routes requests
The component that stores vectors permanently on local disk
The worker that builds indexes on sealed segments
The store that keeps schemas and other metadata
Proxies form the access layer: they check requests, forward them to the right nodes and aggregate partial results.
What do query nodes do in Milvus 2.x?
Load segments into memory and run searches and queries
Assign global timestamps to every incoming write request
Store collection schemas and partition metadata
Serve the web UI for browsing collections
Query nodes hold loaded segments and execute vector and scalar searches; scaling them out raises search throughput.
In a standard Milvus 2.x deployment, which component stores metadata such as collection schemas?
etcd
MinIO
Pulsar
Redis
etcd is the meta store. MinIO or S3 holds data files and Pulsar or Kafka served as the log broker.
Where does Milvus 2.x persist segment data such as binlogs and index files?
In object storage such as MinIO or S3
In etcd next to the collection schemas
Only in the memory of query nodes
In local files on the proxy nodes
Milvus separates storage from compute: segment and index files live in object storage, so nodes can be replaced.
Milvus search throughput is too low while CPU on query nodes is saturated. What helps most?
Adding more query nodes
Adding more etcd members
Creating more partitions
Switching to Strong consistency
Searches run on query nodes, so more query nodes (or replicas across them) spread the load.
In Milvus 2.x you created a collection, inserted data and built an index, but search fails because the collection is not loaded. What is the fix?
Load the collection into memory before searching
Call flush a second time and retry the search
Create a new partition and search that instead
Restart the proxy so it detects the new index
Milvus searches only data loaded into query node memory, so call load_collection (or load) first. release frees that memory.
Which partition does every new Milvus collection start with?
_default
main
partition_0
root
Milvus creates a partition named _default automatically; inserts go there unless you name another partition.
What does marking a scalar field as partition key do in Milvus?
Milvus hashes its values to route entities into partitions
It makes that field the primary key of the whole collection
It forces all values of the field to be unique
It builds a vector index on that scalar field
With a partition key, Milvus manages partitions itself and can prune them when you filter on that field.
Tenant A's data lives in a Milvus partition named tenant_a. How do you search only that data?
Pass partition_names=["tenant_a"] to the search
Set the collection consistency level to Strong
Filter with the expression partition == "tenant_a"
Copy the partition into a new collection first
Search accepts a list of partition names, so only those partitions are scanned.
For an IVF_FLAT index in Milvus, which parameter is set at search time to choose how many clusters are scanned?
nprobe
nlist
nbits
efConstruction
nlist sets the number of clusters when building the index; nprobe sets how many of them each search visits.
Why does Milvus reject a search on an HNSW index with limit=100 and ef=50?
ef must be at least as large as the limit (top-k)
ef must be a multiple of the M build parameter
ef is only valid for IVF index types
HNSW searches allow a limit of at most 50
For HNSW the search parameter ef must be between top-k and its maximum, since the candidate list must hold the results.
Which Milvus index type returns exact results by brute-force comparison?
FLAT
IVF_FLAT
HNSW
IVF_PQ
FLAT compares the query with every vector. IVF_FLAT only scans nprobe clusters, so it is approximate.
Which metric_type values does Milvus 2.4 support for float vector fields?
L2, IP and COSINE
L2, HAMMING and JACCARD
EUCLID, DOT and COSINE
L1, L2 and CHEBYSHEV
Float vectors use L2, IP and COSINE (added in 2.3). HAMMING and JACCARD are for binary vectors.
What is Attu?
An open-source GUI for managing Milvus
The query language used by Milvus
The log broker inside Milvus clusters
The official Python SDK for Milvus
Attu is a web admin tool for Milvus: browse collections, manage indexes, partitions and users, and run test searches without code.
In Milvus 2.x, what is the default consistency level of a new collection?
Bounded
Strong
Session
Eventually
Bounded staleness is the default: reads may miss the latest writes within a small time window, in exchange for lower latency.
A Milvus job inserts data from one process, and a different client must see it in its very next search. Which consistency level guarantees this?
Strong
Session
Bounded
Eventually
Strong waits until all data up to the search timestamp is visible. Session only guarantees a client sees its own writes.
Which Milvus consistency level guarantees a client sees its own writes, but not other clients' latest writes?
Session
Strong
Bounded
Eventually
Session consistency gives read-your-writes for the same client session at lower cost than Strong.
What is a growing segment in Milvus?
A segment still receiving inserts, not yet sealed
A segment whose index is being rebuilt from scratch
A segment copied to every query node as a replica
A segment that compaction is currently merging
New data goes into growing segments. Once sealed (by size, time or flush) they become immutable and get indexed.
What does compaction do in Milvus?
Merges small segments and purges deleted entities
Compresses vectors with product quantization
Moves segment metadata from etcd to MinIO
Splits large collections into partitions
Deletes are first recorded as delete logs; compaction rewrites segments to remove them and reduces the segment count.
What does calling flush on a Milvus collection do?
Seals growing segments and persists them to object storage
Deletes all entities but keeps the collection schema
Drops the vector index so it can be rebuilt later
Releases the loaded collection from the query nodes' memory
Flush forces in-progress data into sealed segments in object storage, which can then be indexed.
chroma: Which Chroma client keeps data only in memory, losing it when the process exits?
chromadb.EphemeralClient()
chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./db")
chromadb.HttpClient(host="localhost")
chromadb.CloudClient(tenant=t)
EphemeralClient (also chromadb.Client()) runs in memory. PersistentClient writes to disk and HttpClient talks to a server.
Which code creates an embedded Chroma client that saves data to the ./chroma folder?
chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma")
chromadb.Client(persist=True)
chromadb.HttpClient(path="./chroma")
chromadb.EphemeralClient(dir="./chroma")
PersistentClient(path=...) runs Chroma inside your process and stores data in that directory.
Which CLI command starts a Chroma server that stores its data in ./db?
chroma run --path ./db
chroma serve --dir ./db
chromadb start --data ./db
chroma server --store ./db
chroma run launches the client-server mode. Applications then connect with chromadb.HttpClient.
By default, which port does a Chroma server started with chroma run listen on?
Chroma serves on port 8000 by default. 6333 is Qdrant, 19530 is Milvus and 5432 is PostgreSQL.
When is Chroma's client-server mode a better fit than embedded mode?
Several services on different machines share one database
A single notebook prototype running on your laptop
A unit test that should leave nothing on disk
A one-off script that runs offline and exits
Embedded mode lives inside one process. A server lets many clients and machines use the same data.
In Chroma, what does create_collection("docs") do when a collection named docs already exists (default arguments)?
It raises an error
It returns the existing one
It overwrites the existing one
It creates docs_1 instead
create_collection fails on a duplicate name unless get_or_create=True. Use get_or_create_collection to reuse it.
Which Chroma method returns a collection if it exists and creates it otherwise?
get_or_create_collection
load_or_create_collection
upsert_collection
ensure_collection
get_or_create_collection is the idempotent way to open a collection at application startup.
What must every record passed to collection.add() in Chroma include?
A unique string id
A precomputed embedding
A metadata dictionary
A document text
ids are required. Embeddings are optional when documents are given, and metadata is optional.
You add documents to Chroma without embeddings and without setting an embedding function. Which model embeds them by default?
all-MiniLM-L6-v2
text-embedding-3-small
bert-large-uncased
clip-vit-base-patch32
Chroma's default embedding function runs the Sentence Transformers model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 locally through ONNX Runtime.
What is the dimension of vectors produced by Chroma's default model, all-MiniLM-L6-v2?
all-MiniLM-L6-v2 outputs 384-dimensional embeddings, smaller than BERT-base (768) or OpenAI ada-002 (1536).
You call collection.add(ids=[...], embeddings=[...], documents=[...]) in Chroma. What happens to the documents?
They are stored as-is and are not embedded again
They are re-embedded and replace your embeddings
The call fails because both were passed
Their embeddings are averaged with yours
When embeddings are provided, Chroma stores them and keeps documents only as text; the embedding function is skipped.
Which Chroma method fetches records by id or metadata filter without any similarity ranking?
collection.get()
collection.query()
collection.search()
collection.fetch_nearest()
get() returns matching records directly. query() performs nearest neighbor search on embeddings or query texts.
Which metadata value does Chroma 0.5 reject for a record?
{"page": 3}
{"draft": True}
{"source": "wiki"}
Chroma 0.5 metadata values must be strings, integers, floats or booleans. Nested dictionaries are not allowed.
Which Chroma query argument keeps only records whose metadata year is greater than 2020?
where={"year": {"$gt": 2020}}
where={"year": ">2020"}
where_document={"$gt": 2020}
where={"$gt": {"year": 2020}}
Metadata filters go in where, with the operator nested under the field name. where_document filters the document text.
Which Chroma filter keeps only records whose document text contains the word pgvector?
where_document={"$contains": "pgvector"}
where={"$contains": "pgvector"}
where={"document": "pgvector"}
where_document={"$eq": "pgvector"}
where_document filters on the stored document text, and $contains performs a substring match.
In Chroma 0.5, how do you require category news AND lang en in a where filter?
{"$and": [{"category": "news"}, {"lang": "en"}]}
{"$both": [{"category": "news"}, {"lang": "en"}]}
{"category": ["news"], "$and": {"lang": "en"}}
{"$all": {"category": "news", "lang": "en"}}
Chroma 0.5 expects one top-level key per where clause, so several conditions are combined with $and (or $or).
What distance function does a new Chroma collection use when you do not configure one?
Squared L2 (Euclidean)
Cosine (angular) distance
Inner product (ip)
Manhattan distance
The default space is l2. You can choose cosine or ip when creating the collection.
In Chroma 0.4 and 0.5, how do you make a collection use cosine distance?
create_collection("docs", metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"})
collection.query(query_texts=q, distance="cosine")
chromadb.PersistentClient(path=p, metric="cosine")
create_collection("docs", distance_fn="cosine")
The space is set with hnsw:space at creation and cannot be changed later; queries do not take a metric argument.
In Chroma query results, what does a smaller value in distances mean?
The record is more similar to the query
The record is less similar to the query
The record was added more recently
The record has fewer metadata fields
Chroma returns distances, not similarity scores, so lower values mean closer matches.
What does collection.query(query_texts=["a", "b"], n_results=3) return in ids?
A list of 2 lists, each with up to 3 ids
A flat list with up to 6 ids in total, best first
A list of 3 lists, each with 2 ids
A single list with the 3 best ids
Query results are grouped per query text, so each field is a list with one inner list per query.
faiss: What kind of search does faiss.IndexFlatL2 perform?
Exact brute-force search over all vectors
Approximate search within a few clusters
Graph-based search over linked neighbors
Search over compressed product codes
Flat indexes compare the query with every stored vector, giving exact results with no training.
Which FAISS index must be trained before you can add vectors?
IndexIVFFlat
IndexFlatL2
IndexFlatIP
IndexHNSWFlat
IVF indexes need centroids learned from data. Flat and HNSW indexes report is_trained as True from the start.
What does calling train() on an IndexIVFFlat do?
Runs k-means to learn the nlist coarse centroids
Builds a navigable small-world graph linking each vector
Normalizes the vectors to unit length
Sorts stored vectors by their L2 norm
Training clusters sample vectors into nlist cells. Each added vector is then assigned to its nearest centroid's list.
What happens if you call add() on an IndexIVFFlat that has not been trained?
FAISS raises an error because the index is untrained
FAISS trains it automatically on the first added batch
All vectors are stored in the first inverted list
The vectors are silently ignored by the index
add() checks is_trained and fails if the coarse quantizer has no centroids yet.
For an IndexIVFFlat, what is the effect of increasing nprobe?
More lists are scanned: higher recall, slower search
More centroids are learned the next time the index trains
Each stored vector uses less memory afterwards
Results are returned with more decimal places
nprobe sets how many inverted lists each query visits. nlist, the number of centroids, is fixed at construction.
What is the default nprobe of a newly created FAISS IndexIVFFlat?
nlist
nprobe defaults to 1, so only the closest cell is scanned. Raising it is usually the first tuning step.
In FAISS, D, I = index.search(xq, 5) where xq has shape (10, d). What are D and I?
Two arrays of shape (10, 5): distances and ids
Two arrays of shape (5, 10): ids and distances
A flat array of 50 distances and one of 50 ids
One array of 10 ids and one of 10 distances
search returns one row per query and k columns: D holds distances and I holds the matching ids.
What does an id of -1 in the I array returned by a FAISS search mean?
Fewer than k results were found for that query
The matching vector was deleted from the index
The match lies at infinite distance from the query
The query vector had the wrong dimension
When a search finds fewer than k neighbors (for example, a low nprobe on an IVF index), missing slots are filled with -1.
What values does faiss.IndexFlatL2 return in the distance array D?
Squared L2 distances
Plain L2 distances
Cosine similarities
Negative inner products
FAISS skips the square root for L2 since it does not change the ranking. Take np.sqrt(D) if you need real distances.
How do you run cosine similarity search with FAISS?
L2-normalize vectors with faiss.normalize_L2, then use IndexFlatIP
Create IndexFlatL2 with an extra metric="cosine" argument
Use IndexIVFPQ with nbits set to 1 for every subvector
Use IndexFlatL2 directly on the unnormalized raw vectors
For unit-length vectors the inner product equals cosine similarity, so normalize both data and queries.
index.add_with_ids fails on a plain IndexFlatL2. What is the usual fix?
Wrap it in faiss.IndexIDMap
Train the index before adding
Switch to faiss.IndexFlatIP
Set index.ntotal manually
Flat indexes only assign sequential ids. IndexIDMap stores your custom 64-bit ids; IVF indexes support them natively.
Which attribute tells you how many vectors a FAISS index currently stores?
index.ntotal
index.d
index.nlist
index.is_trained
ntotal is the vector count. d is the dimension and nlist is the number of IVF cells.
In faiss.IndexIVFPQ(quantizer, d, nlist, m, 8), what must be true of m?
d must be divisible by m
m must be larger than d
m must equal nlist
m must be at least 256
PQ splits each vector into m equal subvectors, so d has to be a multiple of m.
With IndexIVFPQ, d = 128, m = 16 and nbits = 8, how many bytes does each vector's PQ code take?
16 bytes
128 bytes
512 bytes
64 bytes
The code size is m times nbits divided by 8, so 16 bytes, versus 512 bytes for the raw float32 vector.
Compared with IndexIVFFlat, what is the main trade-off of IndexIVFPQ?
Far less memory, but lower accuracy from lossy codes
More memory, but the results become fully exact
No training step is needed, but every search runs slower
GPU-only support, but without any accuracy loss
Product quantization stores compact codes instead of full vectors, so distances are approximations.
Roughly how much RAM do 1 million 768-dimensional float32 vectors need in an IndexFlatL2?
About 3 GB
About 768 MB
About 30 GB
About 300 MB
1,000,000 x 768 x 4 bytes is about 3.07 GB. Flat indexes store the raw vectors with no compression.
With res = faiss.StandardGpuResources(), which call copies a CPU index to GPU 0?
faiss.index_cpu_to_gpu(res, 0, index)
faiss.index_to_device(index, "cuda:0")
index.to("cuda:0", resources=res)
faiss.GpuIndex(index, device=0, res=res)
index_cpu_to_gpu takes the GPU resources, the device number and the CPU index, and returns a GPU index.
What should you do before saving a FAISS GPU index with faiss.write_index?
Convert it with faiss.index_gpu_to_cpu
Train the index again on the GPU
Call index.reset() to free GPU memory
Normalize the stored vectors
write_index serializes CPU indexes, so copy the GPU index back to the CPU first. reset() would erase its vectors.
Why does FAISS on GPU give the biggest speedups when queries are sent in large batches?
Batches let the GPU process many queries in parallel
GPU indexes reject batches with only one query
Batching lowers the memory used by each stored vector
Large batches turn approximate search exact
GPUs are throughput devices; batching amortizes transfer and kernel launch overhead across many queries.
You train an IndexIVFFlat with nlist = 4096 on only 1,000 vectors. What happens?
Training fails: k-means needs at least nlist points
FAISS lowers nlist to 1,000 automatically and trains
Training succeeds and leaves most lists empty
FAISS duplicates points until it has enough of them
k-means cannot learn more centroids than it has points. In practice use many more, tens of points per centroid or more.
pgvector: Which SQL statement enables pgvector in a PostgreSQL database?
CREATE EXTENSION vector;
CREATE EXTENSION pgvector;
LOAD EXTENSION 'vector';
ALTER DATABASE ENABLE vector;
The project is named pgvector, but the extension itself is called vector.
Which column definition stores 1536-dimensional embeddings with pgvector?
embedding vector(1536)
embedding vector[1536]
embedding pgvector(1536)
embedding embedding(1536)
The type is vector with the dimension in parentheses. Square brackets would declare a PostgreSQL array.
Which literal inserts the vector 1, 2, 3 into a pgvector column?
pgvector's text format uses square brackets. Curly braces are PostgreSQL array syntax.
What happens if you insert '[1,2,3]' into a column declared as vector(1536)?
The insert fails with a dimension mismatch error
pgvector pads the vector with zeros to 1536
The column dimension changes to 3
The row is stored but skipped by indexes
A typed vector column enforces its dimension, so inserting a 3-dimensional vector raises an error.
Which pgvector operator returns cosine distance?
<-> is L2 distance, <#> is negative inner product, <+> is L1 distance (0.7.0+) and <=> is cosine distance.
What does SELECT '[0,0]'::vector <-> '[3,4]' return with pgvector?
<-> is Euclidean (L2) distance: the square root of 3 squared plus 4 squared is 5.
What does SELECT '[1,2]'::vector <#> '[3,4]' return with pgvector?
<#> returns the negative inner product (1x3 + 2x4 = 11, negated) so that ascending ORDER BY puts the largest products first.
With pgvector, how do you get cosine similarity, not distance, between embedding and a query vector q?
1 - (embedding <=> q)
embedding <=> q
-1 * (embedding <=> q)
1 - (embedding <-> q)
<=> returns cosine distance, which is 1 minus cosine similarity, so subtract it from 1.
Which query returns the 5 rows nearest to '[3,1,2]' by L2 distance?
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5;
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' DESC LIMIT 5;
SELECT * FROM items WHERE embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' < 5;
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <#> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5;
Nearest neighbors are the smallest distances, so order ascending with LIMIT; this form can also use a vector index.
A table has an HNSW index created with vector_l2_ops, but queries use ORDER BY embedding <=> q. What happens?
The index is not used, because cosine needs vector_cosine_ops
pgvector converts the index to cosine automatically on first use
The query fails with an operator class error
The index is used, with a small loss of recall
An index only serves the operator its operator class was built for, so the planner falls back to a sequential scan.
Compared with IVFFlat, what does pgvector's HNSW index typically offer?
Better speed-recall trade-off, but slower builds and more memory
Faster index builds and less memory, but noticeably lower recall
Exact results, but it requires a separate training step
Lower latency, but it supports only the L2 distance operator
HNSW builds a multilayer graph: queries are faster at the same recall, at the cost of build time and memory.
Why should you create a pgvector IVFFlat index after loading the data rather than on an empty table?
It picks its list centroids from the rows present at build time
PostgreSQL refuses to build any index on an empty table
An IVFFlat index blocks all inserts into the table until rebuilt
Empty IVFFlat indexes are converted into HNSW indexes
IVFFlat clusters existing rows into lists. Built on no data, its lists are poor and recall suffers.
The pgvector README suggests what starting value for lists on an IVFFlat index over 500,000 rows?
For up to 1 million rows the guideline is rows / 1000; above that it is the square root of rows.
Which setting makes a pgvector IVFFlat index scan more lists per query?
SET ivfflat.probes = 10;
SET ivfflat.lists = 10;
SET hnsw.ef_search = 10;
SET ivfflat.nprobe = 10;
ivfflat.probes (default 1) sets how many lists are searched. lists is an index build option, not a session setting.
In pgvector 0.7, with an HNSW index and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, a query uses LIMIT 100. What happens?
It returns at most 40 rows unless ef_search is raised
It returns 100 rows with exactly the same recall
It fails because LIMIT is larger than ef_search
It switches to an exact sequential scan instead
The HNSW scan yields at most ef_search candidates, so set hnsw.ef_search to at least the LIMIT.
In CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64), what does m control?
The max connections per node in each graph layer
The number of lists the vectors are split into
The number of probes used per query at search
The maximum number of dimensions per vector
m (default 16) sets graph connectivity. ef_construction (default 64) sets the candidate list size while building.
In pgvector 0.7, a query with WHERE category_id = 7 ORDER BY embedding <-> q LIMIT 10 uses an HNSW index and returns only 3 rows, though many rows match. Why?
The filter runs after the index scan returns its candidates
HNSW indexes cannot be combined with WHERE clauses
category_id needs to be stored inside the vector
LIMIT is ignored whenever an HNSW index is used
The approximate scan yields ef_search candidates and the WHERE clause then discards non-matching ones. Version 0.8.0 adds iterative scans.
What is a key advantage of pgvector over a standalone vector database?
Vectors sit next to relational data, with joins and transactions
It needs no indexes at all to search millions of vectors fast
It runs vector search on the GPU automatically for every single query
It stores vectors of unlimited dimensions in one column
Embeddings live in ordinary tables, so one SQL query can join, filter and update them under PostgreSQL transactions.
Vector queries usually filter on one of a few category_id values. Which pgvector indexing approach does the README suggest?
A partial HNSW index with WHERE (category_id = 7)
A B-tree index on the embedding column itself
A GIN index on the embedding and category columns
Raising ivfflat.lists to match the row count
A partial index per frequent filter value only contains matching rows, so the approximate scan returns relevant candidates.
Up to how many dimensions can pgvector HNSW and IVFFlat indexes handle for the vector type?
The vector type stores up to 16,000 dimensions, but indexes support up to 2,000; halfvec indexes allow up to 4,000.
